body:
What is a missile?

A missile is a weapon designed to travel towards a target and deliver a payload. In defence technology, the term commonly refers to a powered projectile. A guided missile can determine or correct its direction during flight using a guidance and control system. An unguided rocket, by contrast, receives its initial direction at launch but does not continuously correct its course towards a target.

India develops and evaluates many missile systems through the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). Its Integrated Test Range at Chandipur, Odisha, supports flight testing and measurement of missile performance.

Basic parts and functions

  • Propulsion system: Produces the thrust required to move the missile. Depending on the design, this may be a rocket motor or an air-breathing engine.
  • Navigation system: Provides information about the missile's position, motion or orientation.
  • Guidance system: Determines the required direction of travel using navigation information, commands or information about the target.
  • Control system: Makes the corrections required to follow guidance commands.
  • Seeker: A sensor fitted to certain missiles to obtain information about a target, particularly during the later part of flight.
  • Payload: The equipment or material carried for the intended mission. In a weapon, the payload may include a warhead.

These terms describe different functions. Propulsion moves the missile; guidance determines where it should move; control changes its motion. A seeker supplies target information but is not, by itself, the entire guidance system.

Classification by launch platform and target

Missiles can be classified according to where they are launched and what they are intended to engage. This classification is independent of whether the missile follows a ballistic or cruise-type flight path.

Missile categoryMeaningIndian example
Surface-to-surface missileLaunched from a surface platform against a surface target.Prithvi; land-based Agni variants
Surface-to-air missileLaunched from a surface platform to intercept an aerial target.Akash
Air-to-air missileLaunched from an aircraft against an aerial target.Astra
Air-to-surface missileLaunched from an aircraft against a surface target.Air-launched BrahMos variant
Anti-tank guided missileDesigned primarily to engage armoured ground targets.Nag
Anti-ship missileDesigned to engage ships.Anti-ship BrahMos variant

Some missile families have variants for different launch platforms or target types. Thus, a missile's name does not always identify a single launch platform.

Strategic and tactical roles

Strategic missiles are associated with major national-security objectives, long-range deterrence and the ability to deliver significant effects. Tactical missiles generally support more limited military objectives. This distinction concerns a missile's intended role, not merely its speed or propulsion.

Another independent distinction is the type of warhead: conventional or nuclear. A ballistic missile is not necessarily nuclear, and a cruise missile is not necessarily conventional. The words ballistic and cruise describe flight behaviour, not the nature of the payload.

Prelims focus

  • Akash is a surface-to-air missile system.
  • Astra is an air-to-air missile.
  • Nag is an anti-tank guided missile.
  • Prithvi and Agni are ballistic missile families.
  • BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile with variants for different platforms and roles.
  • Trap: The launch platform, target category, flight path and warhead type are separate classifications.

[Sources: DRDO, 'Missiles and Strategic Systems', organisation and laboratory overview, consulted 14 November 2026; DRDO, 'Akash' and 'BrahMos' product descriptions, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, 'Missile Development Programme', 13 August 2012.]

A launch-platform and target matrix shows four missile roles and examples, with Nag for armoured targets and BrahMos for ships; speed and flight path are separate.

title: Guided Missiles: Meaning, Components and Classification by Role

body:
Ballistic missiles

A ballistic missile receives substantial acceleration from rocket propulsion during an initial powered phase. Much of its subsequent flight is governed primarily by gravity and its existing motion, although some ballistic missiles can also make course corrections.

The word ballistic refers to this general flight behaviour. It does not mean that every ballistic missile follows an identical path or that every modern ballistic missile is completely unguided after launch.

The motion is related to familiar school-level principles. A rocket initially accelerates because it produces thrust. After the powered portion of flight, gravity continues to influence its motion. The longer-range paths of ballistic missiles differ substantially from the simple arc of a thrown ball, but the underlying connection between motion and gravitation remains important.

Cruise missiles

A cruise missile generally sustains powered flight through much of its journey and uses aerodynamic lift while travelling through the atmosphere. Many cruise missiles employ air-breathing engines. They may travel at subsonic or supersonic speeds, depending on the system.

BrahMos is an Indian-Russian supersonic cruise missile. Nirbhay is an Indian long-range subsonic cruise missile development programme. Their different speed categories do not change the fact that both belong to the cruise-missile category.

What does quasi-ballistic mean?

A quasi-ballistic missile has flight characteristics associated with ballistic missiles but may depart from a simple conventional ballistic trajectory. The precise characteristics depend on the system. It should not automatically be classified as a cruise missile.

India's Pralay is officially described as a quasi-ballistic missile. On 5 November 2026, DRDO announced a successful flight test as part of user evaluation trials. The announcement described induction as imminent; it did not say that induction had already been completed.

Missile classification by range

Ballistic missiles are also grouped according to their approximate maximum ranges. Common international categories are shown below. Some publications distinguish additional very-short-range classes, so minor differences in boundary terminology can occur.

CategoryAbbreviationCommon range convention
Short-range ballistic missileSRBMUp to about 1,000 km
Medium-range ballistic missileMRBMAbout 1,000–3,000 km
Intermediate-range ballistic missileIRBMAbout 3,000–5,500 km
Intercontinental ballistic missileICBMMore than about 5,500 km

These are range categories, not categories of launch platform. For example, a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM) is identified by its launch platform, whereas an ICBM is identified by range. A missile may belong to both a platform category and a range category.

Subsonic, supersonic and hypersonic

Speed is often expressed as a Mach number, meaning speed relative to the local speed of sound. Mach 1 is approximately the speed of sound in the surrounding medium; the actual speed in kilometres per hour changes with atmospheric conditions.

  • Subsonic: Slower than the local speed of sound.
  • Supersonic: Faster than the local speed of sound.
  • Hypersonic: Commonly used for speeds of Mach 5 or greater.

Speed alone does not define a missile's complete flight type. A ballistic missile may attain hypersonic speed, but that does not make it a hypersonic cruise missile. Similarly, a supersonic cruise missile remains a cruise missile because of how it sustains flight.

Important distinction: Ballistic or cruise describes the general flight pattern; SRBM or ICBM describes range; subsonic or hypersonic describes speed; surface-to-air or air-to-air describes the launch-and-target relationship.

Prelims focus

  • Agni and Prithvi are ballistic missile families.
  • BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile.
  • Nirbhay is a subsonic cruise missile development programme.
  • Pralay is officially described as quasi-ballistic.
  • ICBM is a range category, while SLBM is a launch-platform category.
  • Trap: Hypersonic speed does not, by itself, establish whether a missile is ballistic or cruise.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19, Chapters 8 'Motion' and 10 'Gravitation'; Missile Defense Advocacy Alliance, 'Ballistic Missile Basics', range classifications, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, 'Successful Trial of Nirbhay Sub-Sonic Cruise Missile', 15 April 2019; 'DRDO conducts successful flight-test of quasi-ballistic missile Pralay', 5 November 2026.]

title: Ballistic, Cruise and Quasi-Ballistic Missiles: Flight, Range and Speed

body:
How does a rocket move?

A rocket moves because it expels material in one direction and experiences a reaction in the opposite direction. This is an application of Newton's third law of motion: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

A rocket carries both its fuel and an oxidiser, a substance that enables the fuel to undergo the chemical reaction that releases energy. Because it does not depend on atmospheric oxygen for this reaction, a rocket can operate outside Earth's atmosphere.

A common misconception is that a rocket must push against surrounding air to move. It does not. Rocket thrust results from the momentum of material expelled from the rocket.

Thrust is the force produced by a propulsion system that drives an object forward. Propulsion is the process that produces this driving force.

Solid- and liquid-propellant rockets

Rocket propellants supply the material and chemical energy needed for thrust. At the school level, the two major categories are distinguished by the physical form in which propellant is stored.

FeatureSolid-propellant rocketLiquid-propellant rocket
PropellantStored in solid form.Stored as liquid fuel and oxidiser.
General characteristicRelatively simple storage and handling arrangement.Uses a more complex fluid-handling arrangement.
Basic advantageSuitable where readiness and comparatively simple construction are important.Can offer substantial control over engine operation, depending on design.

Neither category is automatically more accurate. Accuracy depends primarily on the navigation, guidance, control and other characteristics of the complete missile system. Propellant type alone does not determine a missile's range or effectiveness.

How are air-breathing engines different?

Unlike a rocket, an air-breathing engine takes oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere. It therefore depends on atmospheric air and cannot operate in the same manner in the vacuum of space.

The main types encountered in missile-related current affairs include:

  • Turbojet or turbofan: Jet-engine types that use rotating machinery to compress incoming air. They are associated with sustained powered atmospheric flight.
  • Ramjet: An air-breathing engine in which the forward motion of the vehicle helps compress incoming air. BrahMos uses ramjet propulsion during its sustained supersonic cruise.
  • Scramjet: A specialised air-breathing engine in which combustion occurs while airflow through the combustion region remains supersonic. Scramjet research is associated with hypersonic propulsion.

The distinction between ramjet and scramjet concerns airflow during combustion, not whether the missile is guided. This airflow is subsonic in a ramjet and supersonic in a scramjet. Both describe propulsion technologies.

Indian examples

The Agni family illustrates rocket-propelled ballistic missiles. The BrahMos system illustrates a supersonic cruise missile using ramjet technology. The Nirbhay programme illustrates long-range subsonic cruise-missile development using jet propulsion. DRDO has also pursued indigenous air-breathing propulsion through laboratories such as the Gas Turbine Research Establishment in Bengaluru.

On 18 April 2024, DRDO successfully flight-tested the Indigenous Technology Cruise Missile (ITCM). The official announcement specifically identified indigenous propulsion developed by the Gas Turbine Research Establishment and development led by the Aeronautical Development Establishment. This was a technology and flight-test milestone, not proof that every cruise-missile programme had entered operational service.

Prelims focus

  • Rocket thrust is explained by Newton's third law of motion.
  • Rockets carry an oxidiser and can operate without atmospheric oxygen.
  • Air-breathing engines require oxygen from surrounding air.
  • BrahMos uses ramjet propulsion during sustained cruise.
  • DRDO's ITCM flight test on 18 April 2024 demonstrated an indigenous propulsion system.
  • Trap: Propulsion and guidance perform different functions.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19, Chapter 9 'Force and Laws of Motion', Newton's third law and conservation of momentum; DRDO, 'Missiles and Strategic Systems', propulsion technologies, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, 'Air version of BrahMos supersonic cruise missile successfully test-fired', 8 December 2021; 'India Conducts Successful Flight Trial of Nirbhay Sub-Sonic Cruise Missile', 17 October 2014; 'Indigenous Technology Cruise Missile successfully flight-tested', 18 April 2024.]

pictures.alt: Rockets carry oxidiser and gain thrust by expelling material; air-breathing engines use atmospheric oxygen, with BrahMos and Nirbhay as examples.

title: Missile Propulsion: Rockets, Air-Breathing Engines and Thrust

body:
Navigation, guidance and control are not the same

Navigation provides information about where a missile is and how it is moving. Guidance determines the desired motion from that information and the mission requirements. Control carries out the necessary changes in motion.

A missile may receive some information from its own instruments, some from external systems and some from sensors that observe a target. The exact combination depends on its design.

Inertial and satellite-based navigation

An inertial navigation system (INS) uses onboard instruments to estimate changes in position and orientation from measured motion. It does not require a continuous external radio signal to make these estimates. However, small measurement errors can accumulate over time.

Satellite navigation uses signals from navigation satellites to estimate position. India's regional satellite-navigation system is NavIC. Satellite navigation and inertial navigation can complement each other, but neither term means the same thing as a target-seeking sensor.

Command guidance and homing

In command guidance, a system outside the missile provides guidance commands during flight. The commands may be based on information collected by radar or other sensors.

In homing guidance, the missile uses information associated with the target to guide itself. A seeker is a target-sensing device that may support this function.

Method or sensorBasic principleImportant distinction
Inertial navigationUses onboard measurements of motion.Does not directly identify a target.
Satellite navigationUses navigation-satellite signals to estimate position.Provides location information, not necessarily target identification.
Command guidanceReceives guidance commands from an external system.Depends on communication with that system.
Active radar homingUses radar transmission and reception associated with the missile's own seeker.Differs from receiving only external guidance commands.
Semi-active radar homingUses radar energy illuminating the target from another source.The seeker receives target echoes from an external radar illuminator.
Infrared homingDetects infrared radiation associated with the target.Infrared sensing differs from radar sensing.

What does fire-and-forget mean?

A fire-and-forget missile is designed to continue its engagement autonomously after launch without requiring further guidance from the operator or launch platform. It is still a guided missile.

This does not mean that every fire-and-forget system uses the same seeker or that every guided missile is fire-and-forget. It also does not mean a missile has no need for information before launch.

India's Nag anti-tank guided missile is publicly described as a fire-and-forget system. The Astra beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile has been tested with an indigenous radio-frequency seeker. The Akash Prime and Akash-NG developments also demonstrate the importance of indigenous radio-frequency seeker technology.

Why a seeker matters

A target may be moving, while the missile itself is also moving. Target-sensing systems therefore provide information that a purely position-based navigation instrument cannot supply. Radar and infrared seekers represent different ways of observing a target. Their usefulness depends on the system and circumstances; neither should be considered universally superior.

Prelims focus

  • INS estimates motion using onboard instruments.
  • NavIC is India's regional satellite-navigation system.
  • An active radar seeker uses its own associated radar transmission and reception.
  • An infrared seeker detects infrared radiation.
  • Nag is a fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile.
  • Trap: Fire-and-forget does not mean unguided.

[Sources: DRDO, 'Missiles and Strategic Systems', navigation, guidance and homing systems, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, 'DRDO and IAF conduct successful flight-test of Astra Beyond Visual Range Air-to-Air missile with indigenous Radio Frequency Seeker', 11 July 2025; 'Successful trial of Akash Prime at High-Altitude', 17 July 2025; 'DRDO Successfully Completes User Evaluation Trials of Akash-NG', 23 December 2025; 'Successful Field Evaluation Trials of Nag Mk 2', 13 January 2025.]
